summary: This paper extends prior work on learning logical noise from syndrome data from phenomenological to realistic circuit-level noise models, deriving necessary and sufficient learnability conditions via code-theoretic methods and spacetime code formalism. Efficient estimators using Fourier analysis and compressed sensing are developed with provable sample-complexity guarantees, achieving orders-of-magnitude savings over direct logical benchmarking in estimating logical error probabilities from syndrome data alone.
motivation: Characterizing logical error probabilities in fault-tolerant quantum error correction is essential for device calibration, but direct logical measurements are prohibitively expensive since logical errors are suppressed to higher order. Learning from syndrome data collected during error correction provides a practical alternative to rare event detection.
method: The work establishes a unified theoretical framework using Boolean group algebra and representation theory to characterize learnable degrees of freedom under circuit-level Pauli faults. A circuit-to-spacetime code isomorphism maps syndrome extraction circuits to subsystem codes, enabling application of Fourier analysis and compressed sensing with restricted isometry properties to design efficient learning protocols with optimal sample complexity.
result: The framework achieves $2$–$3$ orders of magnitude reduction in sample complexity for estimating logical error probabilities to $10\%$ relative precision compared to direct logical benchmarking on rotated surface codes (distances $d=3,5,7$) and color codes, with optimal sample scaling $\Theta(\varepsilon^{-1}\tau^{-2})$ for learning prior distributions to precision $\tau\varepsilon$.
